at.step: The lock, and its new failure

syllabus.clause: linearizability as the correctness criterion (Herlihy & Wing, TOPLAS 1990)

at.step: Could a sequential queue do this?

sources.source: Herlihy and Wing, "Linearizability: a correctness condition for concurrent objects" (TOPLAS 1990)

items.item: The L1/L2 definition: extend H to H′ such that complete(H′) is equivalent to a legal sequential history S, and H's real-time precedence order is contained in S's
Locality: a system is linearizable if each individual object is linearizable
Nonblocking: processes invoking totally-defined operations are never forced to wait
Linearizability as a special case of strict serializability restricted to single-operation, single-object transactions; serializability is not local
Wait-free: any process can complete any operation in a finite number of steps, regardless of the execution speeds of the other processes
Bounded wait-free: a fixed bound N on another process's own steps any invocation can remain pending across
Lock-free: ensures only that some thread always makes progress
Obstruction-free: guarantees progress for any thread that eventually executes in isolation, and its own livelock remark: no progress requirement when any interference is detected

sources.source: Gibbons and Korach, "Testing Shared Memories" (SIAM J. Comput. 1997, citation only)

items.item: Checking linearizability in general is NP-complete

expert.by: self-review (no independent reviewer this session; see REVIEW.md)

items.item: Why exactly eighteen of twenty interleavings lose the update: the rule (a read falling inside the other's own read-to-write span) picks out precisely those eighteen, not a rough majority
Why a lock turns every interleaving correct but trades that for an unbounded wait behind a suspended holder — the two failures are not the same failure, and fixing one does not fix the other

at.step: The lock, and its new failure

items.item: Why compare-and-swap's own retry loop can let one thread starve completely while the system as a whole keeps moving — lock-freedom is a system-wide guarantee, not a per-thread one
Why an atomic hardware add sits at the top of the ladder: it finishes in one step regardless of any other thread, which no retry loop, however short, can promise
Why obstruction-freedom is named but not built in this topic: the chapter's own counter only demonstrates blocking, lock-free and wait-free directly, per CHAPTER.md's scope
Why two operations whose intervals overlap in real time have no inherent 'first' — linearizability's whole point is that correctness cannot be read off the clock alone

Why a dequeue returning empty right after a completed enqueue has no legal sequential retelling at all, while an overlapping enqueue/dequeue pair can still have one — the difference is exactly what the L1/L2 definition tests for

Why linearizability composes (locality) while serializability does not: a queue and a map in the same program can be checked one at a time only because of that specific theorem, not as a general property of correctness criteria
That the brute-force checker in examples.py is a research tool at the scale this topic uses it at, not a solution to the general NP-complete problem it is named alongside
Why no claim here says lock-free is always faster than a lock: the only measured example is a scheduling trace, not a contention benchmark, and the post-notes say so explicitly
